steps.content: So, this is how it feels to be in a position like this.
Kisugi Hitomi
Not half bad though.
To defeat your enemy you must know your enemy.
Am I right, Chief?
You turn on the light. For a split second, Sinner Fox's pupils contract.
They look like those of a cunning fox.
Yes.
Pleasure to meet you, Eastside's golden lawyer.
Is that so?
Or maybe, what you really mean is that you've known me quite well?
Mr. Fox shrugs and points at the file in your hand.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Looks like you've done your research on me too.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: I guess we can skip the pleasantries then.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Let's go straight into the problem we're here to discuss.
The Sinner cuts right to the chase even before the interrogation begins. It seems to you that he is confident about how the interrogation will turn out.
Works for me. It'll save us time.

I've received your application for a leave permit...
The reason is... you need to defend a client?

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: That's right.
Mr. Fox says so briskly, adjusting his glasses.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: I took on a case two days before you arrested me as a Sinner.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: My clients count on me to help them seek justice. I can't stand them up.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: One of the MBCC rules stipulates, "If deemed necessary, detention of Sinners who are members of the elite may be suspended to allow the said Sinners to carry out their duties in their respective fields."

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: I count as a member of the elite, I believe?
There is indeed such a rule, and you do count as a member of the elite.
You open the file, which contains documents on the cases taken on by Mr. Fox as a lawyer.
I've gone through the cases you took on. You won every single one of them. That's very impressive.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Thank you.
Just out of curiosity, do you take on every case that comes your way? It's difficult, if not impossible, to win every single case, right?
Mr. Fox hesitates for a split second before answering.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Every lawyer is different. We have different personalities and tastes. We may refuse to take on a case or two occasionally. Nothing unusual about that.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Why? Does it have anything to do with me getting a leave permit?
You don't answer; you only shrug.
But... Mr. Fox, the performance of that rule is subject to certain conditions.
And this is why I'm here today.
I need to do an appraisal before deciding whether we should suspend your detention and allow you to return to Eastside.
Mr. Fox ponders for a long moment before giving a knowing smile.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Fair enough. In your eyes... in the eyes of ordinary folks, we Sinners are way too powerful and dangerous.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: It's like a set of unbalanced scales. The closer one gets to heaven, the more afraid they are of those standing on the opposite end, in the doorway to hell.
That's not the only consideration, Mr. Fox.

I've perused your cases.
I want to know more about some of these cases, so that I can decide whether or not you qualify to go out.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: I won all the cases. Isn't that enough?
I'm afraid not, Mr. Fox.
Let's talk about the copycat case that shocked Eastside not so long ago.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Oh, about that...

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: If I remember correctly, the defendant in this case tried to copy the M.O. of another case, a centuries-old case.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: The detestable criminal in this old case suffered from severe mental illness and harmed similar-looking victims one after another.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: In fact, I once wondered what strategy I would've used to win this case if I had represented one side... or the other.

<size=32>"The suspect in this case, in an attempt to copy the killer in the original case, planned to... harm several females from the same company. They had the same hair, eye, and skin color. But the suspect was caught before the plan was carried out."</size>

"But in the Court of Appeal, the plaintiffs recanted their testimonies and denied the witnesses' statements. They proclaimed that the suspect had been just helping them with their jobs, and that it was purely accidental that they got injured."

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Yeah, those were three unexpected accidents in a row, just like their name suggests, they're the kind of surprises you can stumble upon, but can't really chase after.
Mr. Fox, you represented the defendant in this case, didn't you?

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Yes. A big-eyed girl. My fees are not cheap, so to pay me, she sold everything she owned in the Back Alley...

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Including herself, I might add.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: But I'll never forget the overjoyed look in her eyes when she was acquitted.
Previous to this, the witnesses' testimonies, the evidence gathered from the scene, public opinion... all had pointed to your client committing attempted murder.
You turn to one of the pages which records some of the testimonies for the case.
"The three girls were the defendant's colleagues. The defendant was their senior. They were up for promotion because of their stellar performances."
"Before the incident, they all invited this senior of theirs to a weekend party. And it's at this party that they almost lost their lives."

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: That's not enough to prove that my client was the culprit. Don't you think so?
Mr. Fox adjusts his glasses again, the corner of his mouth lifted by a sardonic smile.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: All the testimonies were recanted in the Court of Appeal.
I've reviewed the court records for the case. The testimonies and evidence the plaintiffs gave after the recantation were almost ludicrous and even self-contradictory.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: So what? Ludicrous or not, testimony can be a lethal weapon, as long as it helps prove my client innocent.
They recanted their testimonies... Was it because of something you did?

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: If you're asking if I visited the witnesses and others who'd give evidence to get the lethal weapon I needed, then yes...

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: I took on the client, which means I would do everything in my power to help her get whatever she wanted.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: The moment the deal was made, I unconditionally believed that my client was innocent.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: If her definition of justice was proof of her innocence, then that's what I'd get her.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Whatever it took...

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: And that's my credo, Chief.
Correct me if I'm wrong, you paid the witnesses to change their stories, or made them do so with your power.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: All for the purpose of getting my client the justice she expected.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Like I said, I'd do everything in my power to prove the client's innocence.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Alas, that gave you a reason to detain me. I understand that you think it's more unforgivable for me to do what I do to get a fellow Sinner like the Countess off the hook than to help a regular Joe escape punishment.
That's not justice, Mr. Fox.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: What is then?

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Spending the rest of her life enduring looks of contempt? Or withering away behind high walls until she becomes as significant as a speck of dust?

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Chief, even those living in hell deserve a lifeline, however thin that lifeline might be.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: For them, justice is victory in court.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: And when the usual courses of action can't bring them what they want, money and my power will...
You snap the file shut and throw it on the table.

I guess there's no need for us to discuss the details of the other cases. The FAC has discovered through their investigation that suspiciously high amounts of money changed hands between you and your clients.
It's also been found that you cut backdoor deals with key witnesses from the opposing side, and that you used your power on many occasions.
Your application is refused, Mr. Fox.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Chief... a defendant, no matter how suspicious-looking, has a right to justice.
Your version of justice comes at the expense of the other party's legitimate interests.
I know about the case you're working on. Your client is the mistress of a manor. She accused one of her maids of poisoning her husband, the patriarch of the manor.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Yes, she pressed charges the day after the husband was found dead and hired me to represent her.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: I hear that the maid is still being locked up in the manor, waiting to be transferred to a prison in Eastside after trial.
With all due respect, I don't think that the maid has anything to gain from the death of the patriarch of the manor.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Chief, you've led many successful missions in Syndicate, don't tell me you don't know that there is more to human nature than meets the eye.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: The truth about human nature is like evidence. You need to guide it, to bring it to light.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Surely you don't want to see justice entombed, never to see the light of day again?
What you've just said makes sense, in a way. But what you do still goes against the current rules. Some restrictions are called for.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: So you're going to refuse my application?
Yes.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Which means I won't be able to appear in court to defend my client...
They will find the lady another lawyer, a more... fair-minded one.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: How she will fare in court is none of my concern now.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Not defending a client in court myself is as good as losing the case.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: I'm a champion of justice. And in my book, justice means an unbroken run of wins.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: I appear in court for each and every one of my clients. I defend them, and I win, as simple as that.
Mr. Fox's expression becomes increasingly somber, and his eyes are fixed on you.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Since you're not signing my permit, I've got no other choice...
An invisible force seems to come off the man before you, pining you down in your seat.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: "Do not fight me, Chief."

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: "Be a dear and do as you're told."
Y-you are using your power against me?

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Uh, ugh...
There is a suggestion of unsteadiness in his searchlight-like eyes.
You notice a dense layer of tiny beads of sweat on the tip of his nose.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Holder of the shackles... you do live up to the name!

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: It's taxing... to force your hand with my power.
You can tell from his expression that there is a build-up of strain inside of him. Then he raises his hands and grasps his neck.
He tightens his grip, as if to force words out of his throat.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: "Take out... my... application form..."

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: "Sign it!"
Mr. Fox's voice is hoarse. Never has he tried to control someone as powerful as the new Chief of the MBCC, someone more powerful than he is.
But he must appear in court for his client, to do his job as a champion of justice.
Under Mr. Fox's steady gaze, you take out the form and sign it.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: "Lift... the restraint... Let me out..."
Mr. Fox is huffing and puffing, his voice as thin as a thread on the point of breaking.
His entire head is throbbing with pain. Bright red liquid streams down his face and gives off a strange metallic smell.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Thank you, Chief.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: And if you don't mind...

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: "Please lift the restraint on me."
You pause for a moment, stand up, and press the button to lift the restraint.

steps.speaker: Mr. Fox
steps.content: Thank you once again.
Mr. Fox's voice is so hoarse that his words are almost unintelligible. He scrambles to his feet, takes a look at you, and makes to walk out of the interrogation room.
Mr. Fox, you should know that it's extremely difficult, if not impossible, for you to control a holder of the shackles.

steps.speaker: Fox
steps.content: "If that's the case, let's meet at the end of heaven."

steps.speaker: Nightingale
steps.content: Chief, you were not actually controlled by Fox, were you?

steps.speaker: Nightingale
steps.content: Why did you sign the permit?
There's no use in keeping him here.
I'm gonna take a trip to Eastside. Miss Nightingale, please get everything ready.
And... find out everything you can on the manor case, and send a copy to my terminal.

steps.speaker: Nightingale
steps.content: Eastside? You want to follow Mr. Fox again?
No, I want to beat him at his own game.
